title: SYSK Selects: Saunas: More Interesting Than You Think!
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2011 episode on saunas. Chuck introduces it as a July pick and notes the correct pronunciation ("sauna," not "sow-na"). Josh and Chuck cover the difference between saunas and steam rooms (dry heat vs. moist heat and evaporation), Finnish sauna culture, savusaunas, electric and wood stoves, rocks like peridotite and olivine-type basalts, infrared saunas, nudity and sauna etiquette across cultures, the physiology of sweating (sweat glands, acetylcholine, toxin excretion, skin benefits, mock fever, immune response), contraindications for pregnancy, heart and blood pressure issues, the history of saunas from Neolithic times through the Middle Ages, their suppression during the Protestant Reformation, and their association with bathhouses and the gay community in the 1970s and 1980s and AIDS. The episode ends with a listener mail about a carbon monoxide leak from an oil furnace that Scott in Connecticut says was noticed thanks to an episode, and a Kiva team plug.
rerun_of: Saunas: More Interesting Than You Think

segments.title: Rerun intro and pronunciation note
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this SYSK Selects rerun from July and explains he is correcting the pronunciation of sauna. Josh opens with a Jolly Rancher sponsor read that turns into banter about purple drank and JaMarcus Russell.

segments.title: Sauna vs steam room
segments.summary: The hosts explain that steam rooms use moist heat at about 104 F, while saunas use dry heat at about 176 F, and why sweat evaporates in a sauna but not a steam room. They note Robert Lamb wrote the original article.

segments.title: Finnish sauna culture
segments.summary: Saunas are a national pastime in Finland, with about 1.6 million saunas and an early description dating to 1113. Finnish military and prison saunas are mentioned, and Chuck recalls childhood sauna use at a Toledo hotel pool membership.

segments.title: Sauna wood, savusauna, and stoves
segments.summary: Cedar and spruce are used because they absorb and release heat and aromatics without getting too hot. The original savusauna is a wood-fired cabin with no chimney, sooty walls, and carbon monoxide risks. Modern saunas use electric or wood-burning kiuas stoves, heated rocks, and water thrown on them for steam (löyly).

segments.title: Infrared saunas and sauna rocks
segments.summary: Sauna rocks must be unweathered quarry rock such as peridotite, hornblende, or basalt, since granite can explode. Infrared saunas use infrared radiation to heat the body directly.

segments.title: Nudity and sauna etiquette across cultures
segments.summary: Nudity norms vary: Finland, Eastern Europe and Russia often expect nudity with a towel to sit on, while Americans wearing bathing suits are frowned upon. Mixed-sex sauna bathing is common in Germany, Austria, Scandinavia and Eastern Europe. Eastern Promises' bathhouse fight is mentioned.

segments.title: Sweat physiology and health benefits
segments.summary: Heat triggers acetylcholine and about 2.3 million eccrine sweat glands. A 15-minute sauna can produce about a liter of sweat. Sweat excretes a small share of toxins such as mercury (about one percent) and benefits skin. Banya users flog themselves with birch or oak branches (vihta/venik), which stimulates circulation and releases endorphins. Saunas produce a mock fever that can raise the immune response. Saunas are not recommended for pregnant women, children, older people, or those with high blood pressure or heart problems, though they may ease menstrual cramps. Hydration is important, and the Finnish tradition of jumping into snow or cold water is discussed, along with the myth about open pores and drowning.

segments.title: History of saunas and the Protestant Reformation
segments.summary: Saunas developed from Neolithic hot-spring settlements and portable sweat-lodge-like structures to dugouts and savusaunas by at least the twelfth century. Medieval villages used them communally, and they became associated with bathhouse prostitution. The Protestant Reformation led to their suppression, and they came back in the late twentieth century, becoming linked with gay bathhouses and the early AIDS epidemic, as depicted in The Band Played On.

segments.title: Sauna etiquette and the world record
segments.summary: Etiquette includes a sauna master (saunamestari) running a strict 10-minute session in Germany, no entering or leaving mid-session, and asking before adding water to the rocks. Timo Kaukonen set a record in 2009, sitting in a 230 F sauna for 3 minutes 46 seconds.

segments.title: Hosts' sauna anecdotes and closing reference
segments.summary: Chuck describes using a sauna at a former job. The hosts close the content with a plug to read the article on HowStuffWorks.com.

segments.title: Listener mail: carbon monoxide leak
segments.summary: Scott in Connecticut writes that a smell of overheated electronics led him to find carbon monoxide from an oil furnace that had imploded. His roommate Caitlin had been asleep watching Colbert upstairs. He credits an SYSK episode on Bhutan's Gross National Happiness, and mentions the Kiva team competition.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck sign off with a call for listeners to send email to the show's address.
